extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners working on computational humor, captioning, and dataset annotation
extracted.subtask_description: A dataset-style collection of cartoon/image-caption examples with structured annotation fields (scene, description, uncanny element, entities, caption, plus an explanation of the joke). Useful for building or evaluating systems that generate or analyze humorous captions.

rubrics_metrics.name: scene
rubrics_metrics.description: A short label identifying the setting of the image (e.g., 'an alleyway', 'a laboratory', 'a rooftop').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplies contextual grounding for the joke; used to situate the caption. Examples on page: 'scene: an alleyway', 'scene: a laboratory'.

rubrics_metrics.name: description
rubrics_metrics.description: A concise prose description of the visible elements and actors in the image (who is present, what they are doing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the literal visual content that a caption will comment on (e.g., 'Two scientists are in a lab, observing a maze. Their lab rat is trying to get to the cheese.'). Used to ensure the caption relates to image content.

rubrics_metrics.name: uncanny
rubrics_metrics.description: A short note pointing out the unexpected, out-of-place, or otherwise incongruous element(s) in the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights the target of the joke (the anomaly to be explained or exploited). Examples: 'The rat has a little jet pack.', 'It is only raining on the man's side.' This field signals likely humor triggers (incongruity, absurdity, literalized metaphor).

rubrics_metrics.name: entities
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of named concepts or things in the image, often linked to Wikipedia (e.g., 'Mouse', 'Jet_pack', 'Maze').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Semantic tags for retrieval, disambiguation, or content filtering. Can be used to match lexical resources or to detect cultural knowledge needed for the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: caption
rubrics_metrics.description: The short punchline or line intended to be the humorous caption for the image (e.g., 'Let's just give him the damn cheese.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary artifact to be produced/evaluated. Captions on the page employ puns, literalizations of idioms, role reversal, dark humor, and other mechanisms. Evaluation should consider relevance to scene/uncanny element and humor effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: A paragraph explaining why the caption is funny — the joke mechanism and how elements in the image map to language/concepts (often pointing out idioms, wordplay, literalization, or incongruity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the rationale and identifies the humor mechanism (e.g., 'A play on the phrase "The Road to Hell is Paved with Good Intentions" — here the street is literally a path to hell.'). Useful as supervision for models and for interpretability of humor types.

rubrics_metrics.name: related_links
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of external links (typically Wikipedia URLs) associated with the image or entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplies background knowledge resources referenced by annotators. Examples: ['https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mouse', 'https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_pack'] — useful to resolve cultural references or world knowledge needed to understand the caption.

rubrics_metrics.name: prompt_questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Open questions presented for the image (e.g., 'Why are they robbing him?', 'What are the two butterflies talking about?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as auxiliary prompts to elicit captions or explanations, or to encourage annotators/generators to consider narrative possibilities. They point to curiosity axes that a good caption may address or subvert.

rubrics_metrics.name: example_id
rubrics_metrics.description: A unique identifier string associated with each example (hex hash-like value visible in the entries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for tracking, referencing, and linking examples across files or annotations (e.g., 'aa255e98af1e246a1cbda578073e2998').

rubrics_metrics.name: numeric_score
rubrics_metrics.description: A numeric value that appears alongside entries (e.g., '68', '86', '74') — likely an annotator-provided rating or internal score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page does not explicitly define this number; it appears consistently and may represent funniness, quality, or an internal identifier. Treat as a numeric attribute but verify provenance before using as a ground-truth 'funniness' label.

rubrics_metrics.name: humor_mechanism (implicit annotations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification of the rhetorical or cognitive mechanism producing the humor (examples found in explanations: literalization of metaphors/idioms, wordplay/puns, role reversal, absurdity, anthropomorphism, dark humor, hyperbole).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not provided as a separate structured field, the explanatory text repeatedly calls out mechanisms. For dataset use, extract or annotate these mechanisms (e.g., 'play on words: feathered', 'literalization: "road to hell is paved"'). These labels are crucial for analysis, generation, and targeted evaluation of humorous strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: caption_acceptability_notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Contextual notes in explanations about social or cultural acceptability of the joke (e.g., references to taboo/dark topics like suicide or beheading are present and explained).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations sometimes acknowledge dark or sensitive content and how it functions in the joke. Use these notes for content warnings, filtering, or assessing appropriateness for target audiences.
